Pioneer Women
Australia's women of 1944 echo in the variety of their activity and ability their pioneer ancestresses of the 18th and 19th centuries: Elizabeth Macarthur, who, at the age of 21, accompanied her turbulent husband to New South Wales in 1789, was herself an innovator in the great sheep industry he founded, and when he was exiled from Australia for nine years managed his estates alone—Mrs. Reiby, who, transported to Sydney in 1792 for a girlish escapade, married a naval officer and carried on the trading business he established—Caroline Chisholm, who, brought up in the atmosphere of slave emancipation and the Factory Acts, founded schools for soldiers' daughters in Madras, and on arrival in Australia in 1838 did fine work for women and girls—Rose Scott, who, born in 1847 and brought up in the bush, campaigned for social justice for women—Lady Windeyer, who figured largely in the Women's Christian Temperance Union and organised the Women's Industrial Exhibition in 1888—her daughter, Margaret Windeyer, who helped to pioneer women's professions, was the first trained librarian in Australia and was largely responsible for the National Council of Women in Australia in 1896.
